progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m6-c12 (burette, pipette, aliquot, titre, concordant titres within 0.10 mL, n = cV, divide by the aliquot); chem-m6-c13 (an indicator signals the endpoint; endpoint and equivalence point are close but not identical); chem-m5-c13 (precipitation, net ionic equations, AgCl white); chem-m5-c14 (Ksp expressions, including a squared term for a 2 : 1 salt); chem-m5-c15 (a solid forms when Qsp exceeds Ksp). Dichromate is named, not taught (its orange colour is not needed).
progression.startsWith: Show why Ag+ first removes chloride. The video opens: This bottle of estuary water looks just like tap water, but it's carrying dissolved salt. How much chloride is in it? You already know how a titration counts acid, with a burette, a pipette and n equals c V.
progression.stopsAfter: writing the titration and indicator equations with colours; explaining why chloride precipitates first and why the chromate amount is controlled; stating the pH condition with both causes and the effect of acid on the titre; naming halide interference and the blank; calculating chloride in mol/L and g/L from concordant titres. No direct or back titration, no hands-on procedure or risk table.
progression.nextLesson: weighing a precipitate instead of measuring a volume (route chem-m8-c02, gravimetric analysis).

teaching.task: Estuary water looks like tap water, but it carries dissolved chloride. With no acid or base for an indicator to respond to, how can a titration with silver nitrate show when the chloride runs out, and how do you turn the titre into a chloride concentration?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) chloride is invisible, and with no acid or base a pH indicator has nothing to respond to; (2) silver forms white silver chloride, 1 : 1, but the white solid gives no stopping signal; (3) a little chromate forms red-brown silver chromate once nearly all chloride is gone, so the first lasting red-brown is the endpoint; (4) chloride goes first because, with lots of chloride and little chromate, silver chloride needs far less silver; as chloride falls, the silver needed rises until red appears; so the chromate amount is set; (5) acid turns chromate to dichromate, so the endpoint is late and the titre high; base gives silver oxide; other silver-precipitating ions count as chloride; the blank corrects the small built-in lateness; (6) chromium(VI) hazard, so the method is often met as data; (7) concordant titres; (8 to 10) titre to moles of silver, 1 : 1 to chloride, divide by the aliquot, then g/L and its meaning.
teaching.conversationalApproach: a bottle of estuary water looks like tap water but carries dissolved salt, and a pH indicator has nothing to respond to because chloride is not an acid or a base, so the video asks how a precipitation titration can measure chloride. Silver nitrate in the burette meets chloride and forms white silver chloride one to one, but the white solid keeps forming right up to the end and gives no signal. A few drops of yellow potassium chromate fix that: while chloride remains the silver makes silver chloride, and once nearly all of it is gone the next silver ions form red-brown silver chromate, the endpoint. Chloride goes first not simply because silver chloride is less soluble but because, with lots of chloride present, its ion product passes Ksp at a much lower silver concentration. The endpoint stays valid only near neutral, since acid turns chromate into dichromate and makes the titre read high. Chromium(VI) is toxic, so the method is mostly met as data. The titres are made concordant and averaged, then the calculation runs one stage at a time: moles of silver from c times V, the one to one ratio, dividing by the aliquot and converting to grams per litre. The memory aid is white while chloride lasts, stop at the first lasting red-brown, then titre, moles, ratio, divide by the aliquot. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: This bottle of estuary water looks just like tap water, but it's carrying dissolved salt. How much chloride is in it? You already know how a titration counts acid, with a burette, a pipette and n equals c V. Chloride isn't an acid or a base, though, so a p H indicator has nothing to respond to. So how do we see the moment the chloride runs out?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) Bore water, 20.00 mL, 0.0250 mol/L AgNO₃, titres 15.10 (rough), 14.62, 14.70, 14.66 mL; find chloride in mol/L and g/L. Tests the concordant mean, n = cV, 1 : 1, the aliquot and g/L. Crossed mistake: doubling the moles with chromate's 2 : 1 ratio (pack trap; site MC distractor). (A2) Pickling-factory wastewater at pH 3, titrated without adjusting pH: explain the effect, suggest a fix. Tests scene 5's cause. Crossed mistake: "No effect: H⁺ isn't in the silver chloride equation" (site MC distractor idea, original wording).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct investigations and/or process data involving:; gravimetric analysis; precipitation titrations" This video processes precipitation titration data (the Mohr method). Gravimetric analysis is chem-m8-c02; practice with both is chem-m8-g01. starts by showing why silver ions remove chloride first, and stops at calculating chloride from a valid Mohr endpoint. It teaches: silver nitrate titrant; Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl (white), 1 : 1; the white solid gives no stopping signal by itself; a little potassium chromate as indicator; after nearly all chloride is used, 2Ag⁺ + CrO₄²⁻ → Ag₂CrO₄ (red-brown); the first persistent red-brown tinge is the endpoint; why chloride precipitates first (each solid forms once its ion product exceeds its Ksp, so the silver concentration each needs depends on the actual chloride and chromate concentrations, not on pure-water solubility); why the chromate amount is controlled; valid conditions (roughly pH 6.5 to 10; acid converts chromate to dichromate and gives a late endpoint and a high titre; strong base gives silver oxide); other silver-precipitating ions counted as chloride; the slightly late endpoint and the blank; the chromate hazard; processing concordant titres (recall); n(Ag⁺) = cV, 1 : 1, divide by the aliquot, mol/L to g/L. Not taught: direct or back titration (M6 recall only), Volhard or Fajans methods, the hands-on procedure and risk table, blank arithmetic, titration curves.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key: silver ions pale grey; chloride green; chromate yellow; silver chloride white tiles; silver chromate red-brown tiles; hydrogen ions soft orange; reasoning lines ink; givens and units navy; the current answer bright; earlier lines dim. Board layout (constant): heading top-left; apparatus left third; inset or board right two thirds. Reuse: painted plates inspected 28 Oct by contact sheet (Assets).
